item.title: Portfolio-aware scenario transfer of reserve movements: evidence from Lloyd's syndicates
item.description: arXiv:2611.08968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A claims-development movement on one portfolio may not transfer directly as a stress to another size. We estimate how to transfer such scenarios between portfolio sizes, using 632 syndicate-years from 117 Lloyd's syndicates over 2015-2024. The measured movement is the change in gross claims estimates on selected older underwriting cohorts, divided by opening gross claims outstanding plus reserves taken on in the year whose development it includes; it is not a pure measure of opening-reserve deterioration. Its dispersion falls materially with reserve size, and a size-based scale predicts held-out syndicates far better than a single market scale. But the transferred upper tail understates the smallest books: in the smallest reserve-size quartile, six of 158 held-out observations exceeded the transferred 99.5th percentile, against 0.79 expected, from three syndicates. Square-root scaling has descriptively lower held-out pinball loss at 99% and 99.5%, though more misses among the largest books. For a GBP 500m portfolio the transferred empirical 99.5th percentile is 0.34 of reserves (95% credible interval, conditional on the fitted model, 0.23-0.52), against 0.67 in the raw market pool. Both are Syndicate 5820's 2016 movement. The contribution is inspectable scenario comparability, not a calibrated capital quantile or a next-year forecast.
item.dc:creator: Colin Priest

item.title: Joint modelling of financial cost and carbon footprint in motor insurance claims: a BINAR(1) decision framework for circular auto parts adoption
item.description: arXiv:2611.09213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motor insurance claims management increasingly faces a dual objective: controlling claim costs while reducing greenhouse-gas emissions associated with vehicle repair decisions. This paper proposes a bivariate, discrete-time modelling framework that links the dynamics of financial claims and repair-related carbon footprint inspired by a BINAR(1) dependence structure, allowing for temporal persistence, cross-dependence and a positive/negative correlation between the two dimensions. Using externally sourced emission factors and cost information for replacement parts, we operationalise the carbon footprint of claims under two repair pathways: new parts versus circular-economy reused parts (PIEC). We then conduct scenario analyses in which the acceptance rate of reused parts varies, and we quantify the joint implications for expected monetary outlays and CO 2 -equivalent emissions. Results show that higher PIEC acceptance can simultaneously reduce expected emissions and average claim cost, and the magnitude of the joint benefit depends on the dependence structure and persistence captured by the BINAR(1) process. The proposed framework provides a transparent, reproducible tool for insurers to evaluate repair-policy levers and to align claims operations with decarbonisation targets while retaining an explicit stochastic risk perspective.
item.dc:creator: Charles Minier (CNP, LSAF), St\'ephane Loisel (CNAM Paris), Renata Alcoforado (UFPE, ULISBOA)

item.title: Correlation Ambiguity, Diversification Fragility, and Insurance Pricing
item.description: arXiv:2603.18969v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study how correlation ambiguity affects insurance supply, investment, and pricing in a competitive market. An insurer jointly chooses underwriting and risky investment under worst-case correlation uncertainty, with the insurance loading determined by insurance supply and household demand. With the correlation midpoint and all other model parameters fixed, widening the correlation interval makes diversification less reliable. With underwriting fixed, absolute financial investment weakly declines; with endogenous underwriting, investment may instead rise as insurance supply contracts. Nevertheless, joint exposure to uncertain dependence, measured by underwriting times absolute financial investment, strictly decreases whenever positive. Once this exposure vanishes, further ambiguity leaves the equilibrium unchanged. Insurance prices redistribute ambiguity costs between insurer and policyholder, while combined local certainty-equivalent surplus declines as long as joint exposure remains positive.
item.dc:creator: Peiyun Deng, Shunzhi Pang

item.title: Universal Value-at-Risk superadditivity
item.description: arXiv:2606.22884v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Value-at-Risk (VaR) is a standard regulatory risk measure, and its failure of subadditivity is well known. Much less appreciated is that for sufficiently heavy-tailed losses, VaR can be superadditive uniformly across all probability levels, a phenomenon strictly stronger than the asymptotic superadditivity studied in extreme value theory. We call this property universal VaR superadditivity (UVS). We study UVS and its stronger weighted version (WUVS) as properties of random vectors rather than of marginal distributions. This perspective unifies and extends a recent line of work on iid infinite-mean models. UVS, except for trivial cases, imposes an infinite-mean structure. We establish preservation properties of UVS and WUVS under increasing and convex transformations, weak convergence, and certain distributional mixtures, and use these tools to prove UVS and WUVS for non-identically distributed risks in several large families including completely subscalable, super-Cauchy, and inverted subadditive risks, extending results previously available only in the iid case. In many results, we also establish strict versions of UVS and WUVS, which lead to stronger decision-theoretic implications. As a consequence, for any portfolio satisfying WUVS, every distortion risk measure is superadditive, so an optimal allocation concentrates on a single asset, and diversification is never beneficial.
item.dc:creator: Yuyu Chen, Liyuan Lin, Ruodu Wang

item.title: Shared AI Decision Interfaces and Credit Allocation in a Simulated Lending Market
item.description: arXiv:2610.15973v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language-model agents can choose from a shared menu of actions. I ask whether the order of that menu, which carries no payoff-relevant information, can move credit in a market. Borrowers from three small open-weight model families operate in a simulated collateralized lending market. In each of 12 matched blocks, one market shows all borrowers the same complete action order and the other balances the six orders. An exact randomization test, hash-locked locally before the first model call, rejects the null that common-market net debt does not depend on the assigned order (two-sided p = 2/8,100). The pre-specified lever-up-first versus delever-first estimate is 1.12 units of initial unused borrowing capacity. Every lever-up-first market ended above the balanced market of its block, and every delever-first market ended below it. Exploratory counterfactuals show why the collateral cap does not undo this shock. The cap limits new borrowing, but no rule makes a borrower sell collateral. The market's rules therefore keep 41 percent of the borrowing difference and 93 percent of the repayment difference. Pool-price valuation also returns part of the screened borrowing. Exposure responds more than debt. Lever-up-first markets ended with 58 percent more debt than delever-first markets and about four times the scenario write-offs under a fixed-price shock (exploratory p = 2/8,100). Credit decisions were concentrated as well, because one model family bought 86 percent of the tokens purchased on credit. No market had a liquidation or realized bad debt.
